pages.x: Pharaohs had dug canals from the Nile to the Red Sea, but ships sailing from Europe to Asia still had to go all the way around Africa. In 1854 the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps won leave from his friend Said Pasha, the ruler of Egypt, to dig a canal straight across the desert isthmus of Suez.

Lesseps was no engineer, but he was a brilliant salesman. Britain, afraid of French power on the road to India, fought the plan, so he sold shares to thousands of ordinary French savers, and Egypt bought most of the rest. Work began in April 1859 on the beach where Port Said now stands.

For years most of the digging was done by Egyptian peasants forced to work in the heat with picks and baskets, and many died of disease. After protests in Europe the forced labour was stopped in 1864, and huge steam dredgers took over.
pages.of: peasants made to dig at any one time

pages.x: The canal opened in November 1869 with fireworks, balls and a procession of ships led by the French empress Eugénie in her yacht. Egypt's ruler, Ismail, spent a fortune on the party and built an opera house in Cairo, for which Verdi wrote Aida, his opera of ancient Egypt, first sung there in 1871.
A channel at sea level, 164 kilometres long and with no locks, joining the Mediterranean to the Red Sea.
pages.fx: The voyage from London to Bombay was cut by about two fifths. Steamships took over from sailing ships, and trade between Europe and Asia boomed.

pages.x: Ismail ran up huge debts, and in 1875 he had to sell Egypt's shares. The British prime minister, Benjamin Disraeli, bought them within days with a loan from the Rothschild bank. In 1882 Britain invaded Egypt, and its troops stayed for more than 70 years to guard the canal and the road to India.

In 1956 Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, took the canal into Egyptian hands. Britain, France and Israel invaded, but the United States and the Soviet Union forced them to pull out. It was a sign that the age of the European empires was over.

The Suez Canal remade the map of world trade. Today about a tenth of the world's seaborne trade passes through it, and when a giant container ship stuck fast across it for six days in 2021, supply chains around the world felt it.
